_partNote: The seven tiles use seven different form factors so they read apart in one row: a tall thin standing rocket, a schematic globe with one inclined ring, a box bus with two flat wings, a deep bowl-shaped dish, a stout open-mouthed telescope barrel, a thin flat rectangular slab terminal, and a squat drum-shaped tug. Class 2 is an abstraction rather than an object, so it uses a plain geometric globe with a single tilted ring and one small satellite on it, kept schematic instead of illustrative; the dish in class 4 and the flat panel in class 6 are deliberately opposite shapes so the two antenna classes do not collide.

partPrompts.1: A slender launch vehicle standing vertical on a flat pad, seen three-quarter: a tall smooth cylindrical body of constant diameter capped by a pointed conical payload fairing at the top, with a slightly wider engine section at the base holding a cluster of small bell nozzles and four stubby fins. Very tall and thin, one object standing alone. No launch tower, no gantry, no flame, no exhaust, no smoke, no ground vehicles.
partPrompts.2: A simple geometric globe: a plain sphere marked only with a few evenly spaced latitude and longitude lines, encircled by one thin ring tilted at an angle to those lines, with a single small box-shaped satellite riding on the ring. The ring is a clean continuous circle that passes behind the sphere on one side and in front of it on the other. Schematic and geometric, with no continents, no coastlines, no clouds, no stars and no second ring.
partPrompts.3: A satellite bus seen three-quarter: a plain box-shaped spacecraft body sitting square to the viewer, with two flat rectangular solar array wings extending straight out from opposite sides on short hinged arms, each wing divided into three panels by simple straight lines. Symmetrical, low part count, the box and the two flat wings the whole silhouette. No dish, no reflector, no telescope, no booms and no robotic arm.
partPrompts.4: A parabolic reflector antenna on a simple two-legged mount, seen three-quarter: one deeply concave circular dish, clearly bowl-shaped in profile, with a short straight arm rising from the center of the bowl to a small horn at the focus, carried on a low base. The curve of the bowl is the point and must read clearly from the side. Not a flat plate, not a rectangular panel, no solar wings, no box-shaped spacecraft body.
partPrompts.5: A space telescope barrel standing upright on a square mounting frame, seen three-quarter: a stout cylindrical tube, open at the top, with a stepped conical sunshade widening out of the open end so the aperture reads as an open circular mouth. A few plain stiffening rings run around the barrel. One thick short tube, not a rocket: no nose cone, no nozzle, no fins, no dish.
partPrompts.6: A flat-panel satellite user terminal seen three-quarter: a thin rectangular slab with a completely flat featureless face and square corners, propped at a shallow tilt on a short folding kickstand foot, with a single cable leaving the base. The face is planar with a narrow border around it. No bowl, no curve, no dish, no parabola, no solar wings, no box-shaped spacecraft.
partPrompts.7: An orbital transfer vehicle seen three-quarter: a squat drum-shaped spacecraft, wider than it is tall, with a flat circular payload adapter ring on its top face, four small nozzle stubs spaced around its lower edge, and a short blunt docking probe projecting from one side. Compact and cylindrical. No solar array wings, no dish, no payload fairing, no large bell nozzle and no robotic arm.
